![The talk's title slide. Image from [Maciej Cegłowski's talk](https://idlewords.com/talks/superintelligence.htm).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="cover-full.jpg"}

In a [2016 talk](https://idlewords.com/talks/superintelligence.htm) at Web Camp Zagreb, [Maciej Cegłowski](https://idlewords.com/), who runs the bookmarking service [Pinboard](https://pinboard.in/), argues that belief in machine superintelligence is "the idea that eats smart people": a chain of individually plausible premises that, followed to the end, turns capable engineers into a quasi-religious movement. He opens with the 1945 worry that the first atomic-bomb test might set the atmosphere on fire, a fear physicists could rule out because the underlying nuclear laws were well understood, and uses it as the foil for the AI version of the same fear: a "runaway reaction" in which a machine reaches and then exceeds human intelligence in a very short span. His target is [Nick Bostrom](https://nickbostrom.com/)'s *Superintelligence*, the 2014 book that synthesizes the alarmist case and that Stephen Hawking, Elon Musk, and a raft of Silicon Valley investors found persuasive.

**The premises.** The talk first lays out the six assumptions Bostrom's intelligence-explosion argument needs:

- *Proof of concept*: thinking minds exist, so the thing is possible in principle.
- *No quantum shenanigans*: the brain is ordinary matter that could be emulated, with no quantum magic required (contra [Roger Penrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Penrose)).
- *Many possible minds*: the space of possible minds is large, and no physical law caps intelligence at the human level. A motorcycle outruns any cheetah, but evolution had to build humans first before anything could build the motorcycle.
- *Plenty of room at the top*: hardware still has room to get much smaller and faster.
- *Computer-like time scales*: software would run on machine time scales, vastly faster than human thought.
- *Recursive self-improvement*: an AI could improve itself, looping into a runaway takeoff.

**The rebuttals.** He then attacks the takeoff scenario from about a dozen angles, most named for a memorable image:

- "Intelligence" has no agreed definition, and may not even be a single quantity you can maximize.
- *Stephen Hawking's cat*: a huge intelligence advantage doesn't let Hawking talk a cat into its carrier, and a disembodied AI has the same problem, it must persuade humans to act for it. *Einstein's cat* and the Australian *[Emu War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emu_War)* extend the point: even brute force, or coordinated humans with machine guns, can be defeated by far less intelligent creatures.
- *Slavic Pessimism*: we can't write secure software (he cites an Ethereum contract that was exploited to drain tens of millions), so expecting to code a stable moral fixed point that survives thousands of rounds of self-modification, correctly, on the first try, doesn't match any experience we have.
- *Complex Motivations*: against the [Orthogonality Thesis](https://nickbostrom.com/superintelligentwill.pdf) and its paperclip maximizer, he argues that complex minds probably have complex motivations, and would sooner write poetry about paperclips than tile the universe with them.
- *The Argument From Actual AI*: real progress comes from pouring massive amounts of data into relatively simple, opaque neural networks, which offer no place to recursively tweak short of retraining on more data.
- The *roommate*, *brain surgery*, *childhood*, and *Gilligan's Island* arguments push the same way: raw intelligence doesn't imply a drive to self-improve or conquer, it is massively interconnected rather than a tunable module, it develops slowly through interaction with the world, and it is distributed across an entire civilization rather than sitting in one mind.

**The outside arguments.** The second half is about what believing all this does to a culture:

- *Grandiosity*: enormous payoffs multiplied by tiny probabilities, used to justify almost anything.
- *Megalomania*: fixing the world by building a God-machine. The talk quotes [Joi Ito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joi_Ito) on the people doing it:

  > This may upset some of my students at MIT, but one of my concerns is that it's been a predominantly male gang of kids, mostly white, who are building the core computer science around AI, and they're more comfortable talking to computers than to human beings. A lot of them feel that if they could just make that science-fiction, generalized AI, we wouldn't have to worry about all the messy stuff like politics and society. They think machines will just figure it all out for us.
- *Religion 2.0*: the singularity as a nerd apocalypse offering immortality and even resurrection.
- *Comic-book ethics*: a few lone heroes charged with saving the world, an industry of rich men who think they are Batman.
- *Simulation fever*: the same reasoning, taken far enough, concludes we already live in a simulation.
- *Data hunger*: the surveillance economy as a byproduct of data-hungry AI.
- *AI cosplay*: people behaving like their own fantasy of a hyperintelligent agent.

His own position: our understanding of the mind is roughly where alchemy was in the 1600s, diligent but missing the key tools, and the pressing risks are mundane, people exploiting people, carelessness baked into automated systems, and surveillance, not a machine takeover.

## My Notes

- **Ito's demographic claim held up.** The talk quotes Joi Ito on AI being built by a "predominantly male" and "mostly white" group, which in 2016 sounds like an offhand provocation. The measurements that came soon after support it. [Nesta's study](https://www.nesta.org.uk/report/gender-diversity-ai/) of arXiv AI papers found only 13.8% of authors are women, with no improvement in the share of woman-authored papers since the 1990s. The [AI Now Institute's *Discriminating Systems*](https://ainowinstitute.org/publication/discriminating-systems-gender-race-and-power-in-ai-2) report counted women as 18% of authors at major AI conferences and more than 80% of AI professors as men, and put Black workers at 2.5% of Google's staff and 4% at Facebook and Microsoft. Both are 2019 figures, but because that share had been flat for decades, the imbalance Ito named looks structural rather than a snapshot. More recent workforce counts run somewhat higher, though women remain a clear minority of AI researchers.

## Related Posts

- [Recursive Superintelligence's $4B Bet on Self-Improving AI](/posts/20260526-recursive-superintelligence-launch/): the recursive self-improvement the talk rebutted in 2016 is now a funded category, a $4B+ lab betting on automating AI research itself.
- [Yann LeCun on What Comes After LLMs](/posts/20260523-yann-lecun-after-llms/): another skeptic who calls LLMs a dead end for human-level intelligence and locates the danger in mundane failure modes rather than a takeover, the same split the talk draws.
- [Karpathy: AGI Is Still a Decade Away](/posts/20251018-karpathy-agi-decade-away/): a working researcher's version of the "Argument From Actual AI," doubtful that models training on their own outputs lead anywhere but collapse.
- [Math Is AGI: Carina Hong on Axiom and Formal Reasoning](/posts/20260514-carina-hong-axiom-math-is-agi/): the believer side, a commercial pitch treating AGI as both imminent and the most important thing to build, the conviction the talk calls grandiosity.
